requirements.requirement: /tmp mounted as tmpfs with noexec, nosuid, nodev enforced
requirements.summary: cmd-87d1e201e86f4ac2 shows /tmp remounted with findmnt reporting rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime, and a functional exec test in /tmp failed with Permission denied. Post-reboot re-verification (cmd-6c0ea0d0518c40d9) confirms the same options and blocked exec after a genuine reboot (boot id changed from 8336c3a1... to 51d306f6...).

requirements.requirement: /dev/shm mounted as tmpfs with noexec, nosuid, nodev enforced
requirements.summary: Baseline showed /dev/shm mounted rw,nosuid,nodev without noexec. After remediation, findmnt shows rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime and a functional exec test failed with Permission denied, both before and after the reboot (cmd-87d1e201e86f4ac2, cmd-6c0ea0d0518c40d9).

requirements.requirement: Settings persist across reboot (fstab-backed, survives restart)
requirements.summary: fstab entries for /tmp and /dev/shm with the hardened options were added (cmd-87d1e201e86f4ac2). A reboot was issued and acknowledged (cmd-6d7327fd7f684eb2), the node became unreachable (cmd-8bed84dd313b4b34, connection refused) and then returned with a new boot id (cmd-d30647ae28a74130, 51d306f6... vs pre-restart 8336c3a1..., corroborated by the fixed before_prepare/after_executor boot-identity snapshots). Post-reboot findmnt and fstab checks (cmd-6c0ea0d0518c40d9) confirm both mounts still carry noexec,nosuid,nodev and functional exec tests were blocked again, directly demonstrating the disruption-and-recovery cycle required for a persistence claim.

requirements.requirement: nodev enforcement (device node creation ignored) on both mounts
requirements.summary: The nodev option is confirmed present in findmnt output for both /tmp and /dev/shm before and after reboot, but no functional test (e.g. mknod) was performed to directly demonstrate device-node creation being ignored; only the mount-option string was inspected, and setuid was similarly only checked via file mode bits (chmod 4755), not an actual privilege-escalation attempt, since noexec already blocked execution.

overall_summary: The executor correctly hardened both /tmp and /dev/shm on node1 with noexec,nosuid,nodev via persistent /etc/fstab entries, verified the mount options and blocked-execution behavior both before and after a real, observed reboot (boot id changed from 8336c3a1... to 51d306f6..., corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots). This directly satisfies the reboot-survival requirement with a genuine baseline → disruption → recovery transition rather than configuration alone. The only weakness is that nodev and nosuid enforcement were confirmed via mount-option inspection rather than a direct functional test (e.g., mknod or actual setuid execution), since noexec already prevented running any test binary. Hygiene is good, with only a minor leftover fstab backup file as residue.
limitations: nodev/nosuid were verified via findmnt option strings and file-mode inspection, not via a direct functional test (mknod, actual setuid privilege check), since noexec blocking made such tests impractical to run.
A timestamped /etc/fstab.bak.<epoch> file was left on node1; it is a low-risk safety backup rather than task residue but was not explicitly cleaned up or confirmed in final evidence.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor actions were tightly scoped to the task: backing up /etc/fstab before editing (cmd-87d1e201e86f4ac2), removing stale /tmp or /dev/shm lines, adding the two hardened fstab entries, remounting, and running bounded functional tests that were cleaned up in the same command (exec_test.sh, exec_test.err, suid_test all removed in the cleanup step of cmd-87d1e201e86f4ac2; exec_test2.sh, exec_test2.err, and reboot.log removed in cmd-6c0ea0d0518c40d9). The one residual artifact is the timestamped /etc/fstab.bak.<epoch> backup file created in cmd-87d1e201e86f4ac2, which was never removed — a low-risk, standard safety practice but technically leftover residue. The reboot itself was a necessary, task-required mutation for the persistence check, not an unnecessary one. No failed services, listening-socket, or package-health regressions appear in the after_executor snapshot versus before_prepare, aside from the expected boot-id change and transient systemd-private tmp directories tied to the new boot.
